The system ensures that every patient action is processed in real time and translated into meaningful feedback and stored data for clinical evaluation.

### **3.5.2 Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)**

The Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) presents the logical structure of the TheraQuest VR database by defining the relationships between entities involved in the rehabilitation system. It illustrates how data is organized, stored, and connected, particularly focusing on patients, therapists, rehabilitation sessions, motion tracking data, and performance records. The ERD ensures that all system data is properly structured to support efficient storage, retrieval, and analysis of rehabilitation progress and adherence monitoring.

**Figure 3.5.2.1** Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) of the TheraQuest VR System

The **Physical Therapist** entity serves as the root of the database structure and stores essential profile information, including the therapist's unique identifier (**therapist\_id**), which serves as the primary key, along with the therapist's name and area of specialization. As the primary clinical authority in the system, the physical therapist is directly associated with both patients and rehabilitation programs, establishing the therapist as the central point from which all rehabilitation activities originate.

The **Patient** entity stores personal information about each individual undergoing rehabilitation, including a unique patient identifier (**patient\_id**) as the primary key, the **therapist\_id** as a foreign key linking the patient to their assigned physical therapist, and additional demographic attributes such as name, age, and gender. This relationship establishes that one physical therapist may be responsible for managing multiple patients, reflecting the one-to-many relationship between the Physical Therapist and Patient entities.

The **Rehabilitation Program** entity represents the structured therapy plan designed and assigned by the physical therapist. Its attributes include a unique program identifier (**program\_id**) as the primary key, the **therapist\_id** as a foreign key that associates the program with its creator, along with the program name and description. This entity reflects that a single physical therapist may design and manage multiple rehabilitation programs, each tailored to specific therapeutic goals or patient conditions.

The **Exercise** entity contains the individual therapeutic activities that are included within a rehabilitation program. Each exercise is identified by a unique **exercise\_id** as the primary key and references its parent program through the **program\_id** foreign key. Additional attributes include the exercise name, step-by-step instructions, and the required movement that defines the expected physical action for that exercise. This entity establishes a one-to-many relationship with the Rehabilitation Program entity, meaning that each program is composed of multiple exercises.

The **Session** entity represents each rehabilitation session performed by a patient. It is identified by a unique **session\_id** as the primary key and contains two foreign keys: **patient\_id**, which links the session to the patient who performed it, and **program\_id**, which identifies the rehabilitation program being followed during that session. Additional attributes include the session date, start time, end time, and completion status, which collectively provide a full record of each therapy activity. The Session entity serves as the central transactional entity in the database, as it connects patient activity with both the rehabilitation program and the evaluation records generated during the session. One patient may have many sessions over the course of their rehabilitation, and each session follows a specific rehabilitation program.

The **Adherence Record** entity tracks whether a patient has completed an assigned rehabilitation session. It is identified by a unique **adherence\_id** as the primary key and references the corresponding session through the **session\_id** foreign key. The **completion\_status** attribute records whether the session was fully completed or left incomplete. This entity maintains a direct one-to-one relationship with the Session entity, ensuring that every session has a corresponding adherence record that the physical therapist can review to monitor patient compliance with prescribed therapy requirements.

The **Performance Record** entity stores the evaluated results generated from each exercise performed during a session. It is identified by a unique **performance\_id** as the primary key and contains two foreign keys: **session\_id**, which links the record to the session in which the exercise was performed, and **exercise\_id**, which identifies the specific exercise being evaluated. The remaining attributes include the accuracy score reflecting how correctly the patient performed the movement, the system-generated feedback provided during or after execution, and a timestamp indicating when the evaluation was recorded. This entity captures a detailed, exercise-level evaluation for each session, establishing a many-to-many bridge between the Session and Exercise entities through its foreign key references.

Overall, the ERD demonstrates a well-structured and relational database design that supports all functional requirements of the TheraQuest VR system. The Physical Therapist entity anchors the clinical hierarchy, while the Session entity serves as the operational core that connects patient activity, program adherence, and performance evaluation. Together, the entities and their relationships ensure that all rehabilitation data, from program design to session execution and performance assessment, is systematically stored, retrievable, and aligned with the system's objectives of motion tracking, real-time feedback, and adherence monitoring.

### **3.5.3 Data Flow Diagram (DFD)**

The Data Flow Diagram (DFD) illustrates how data moves through the TheraQuest VR system, from input collection to processing and output generation. It provides a visual representation of how user data, such as movement and interaction inputs, is transformed into meaningful outputs, including feedback, performance metrics, and adherence reports. The DFD highlights the interactions among external entities, system processes, and data storage, ensuring a clear understanding of how information flows through the system.

#### **A. Level 0 DFD (Context Diagram)**

The purpose of the **Level 0 Data Flow Diagram** is to clearly establish the overall scope and external interactions of the TheraQuest VR system by representing it as a single, unified process. At this level, the diagram defines the **system boundary**, which distinguishes what is considered part of the system from what exists outside of it. The TheraQuest VR system itself is enclosed within this boundary and is treated as a “black box,” meaning that its internal processes, such as motion tracking or feedback generation, are not yet shown. Instead, the focus is on how the system communicates with external actors.

![][image6]

**Figure 3.5.3.1** Context Diagram of the TheraQuest VR System

Within this context, the diagram identifies the **external entities** that interact with the system but are not part of its internal structure. In this study, these entities include the patient and the physical therapist. The patient engages directly with the VR environment by performing rehabilitation exercises, thereby providing movement and interaction data to the system. In return, the system delivers real-time feedback and guidance to assist the patient in performing the exercises correctly. On the other hand, the physical therapist interacts with the system by supplying rehabilitation parameters, such as prescribed exercises and movement requirements. The system processes this input and generates corresponding outputs in the form of performance metrics and adherence reports, which are then returned to the therapist for evaluation and monitoring.

The diagram also illustrates the **major data flows** between these external entities and the system. These data flows represent the movement of information into and out of the system, emphasizing what type of data is exchanged rather than how it is processed. For example, movement data flows from the patient to the system, while feedback flows back to the patient. Similarly, rehabilitation parameters flow from the therapist into the system, and performance or adherence reports flow back to the therapist. By focusing only on these high-level exchanges, the Level 0 DFD provides a clear and simplified view of how the system interacts with its environment, without introducing the complexity of internal operations.

#### **B. LEVEL 1 DFD**

The **Level 1 Data Flow Diagram** expands the Context Diagram by decomposing the TheraQuest VR system into its major internal processes to show how data is handled within the system rather than only between external entities. Unlike the Level 0 view, which represents the system as a single process, this level illustrates how user inputs are processed through key functions such as motion tracking, exercise evaluation, feedback generation, and adherence monitoring, allowing a clearer understanding of how raw movement data is transformed into meaningful outputs like real-time feedback and performance results. It also introduces the system’s database as a central data store where user records, session data, performance metrics, and adherence information are saved and retrieved as needed. External entities such as the patient and physical therapist remain part of the diagram, but their interactions are now linked to specific processes, showing how patient movements flow into the system and how feedback is returned, while therapists provide rehabilitation parameters and receive generated reports. This level of representation provides a more detailed view of system behavior and clarifies how each functional component contributes to the overall data flow and system operation.

![][image7]

**Figure 3.5.3.2** Data Flow Diagram of the TheraQuest VR System

The process begins when the **Patient (User)** performs rehabilitation movements within the VR environment. These movements are captured and transmitted as **Movement Data** to the **Motion Tracking module**, which is responsible for detecting and interpreting body posture and motion using computer vision techniques. The processed motion data is then forwarded as **Processed Motion Data** to the **Exercise Evaluation module**.

Within the Exercise Evaluation process, the system compares the user’s movements against predefined rehabilitation standards provided by the **Physical Therapist**, referred to as **Rehabilitation Parameters**. Based on this comparison, the system generates **Evaluation Results**, which determine the accuracy and quality of the performed exercises.

The Evaluation Results are then distributed to two key processes. First, they are sent to the **Feedback Generation module**, which produces **Real-Time Feedback** that is returned to the patient through the VR interface to guide corrections and improvements during exercise execution. Second, the results are sent to the **Adherence Monitoring module**, which records **Session Performance Data** to determine whether the user has completed the required rehabilitation activities.

Both performance-related outputs and adherence records are stored in the **Database**, where they are managed as **Performance Metrics** and **Adherence Records**. These stored data are later retrieved by the system and compiled into **Performance and Adherence Reports**, which are provided to the **Physical Therapist** to support clinical assessment and monitoring of patient progress.

## **3.6 System Design and Architecture**

System design and architecture present the overall structure, organization, and technical arrangement of the TheraQuest VR system. This section explains how the system’s components, layers, modules, and processes are designed to work together in supporting VR-based rehabilitation. It serves as the blueprint for system implementation by showing how user interaction, motion tracking, exercise evaluation, feedback generation, gamification, adherence monitoring, and data management are integrated into one functional rehabilitation platform.

### **3.6.1 System Flowchart**

The system flowchart illustrates the step-by-step processes involved in the operation of the TheraQuest VR system. It shows the sequence of user interactions from system access to exercise execution, motion tracking, evaluation, feedback generation, and session completion. This provides a clear view of how inputs are processed into outputs and ensures that the system workflow is organized and aligned with its functional requirements.

**Figure 3.6.1.1** System Flowchart of the TheraQuest VR

The system flowchart illustrates the overall operational process of the **TheraQuest VR system**, beginning from user login and continuing through two possible user paths: the **Patient workflow** and the **Physical Therapist workflow**. It shows how the system manages authentication, rehabilitation exercise execution, motion analysis, feedback generation, adherence recording, and therapist monitoring.

The process begins when the user starts the system and proceeds to the **Log In** step. After entering login details, the system validates the user’s credentials to confirm access. Once validated, the system determines whether the user is a **Patient** or a **Physical Therapist**. This decision point separates the system into two major workflows based on the role of the authenticated user.

For the **Patient workflow**, the system loads the assigned rehabilitation program created by the physical therapist. The patient then starts the VR rehabilitation session and performs the required exercises inside the virtual environment. As the patient moves, the system captures body movement data and analyzes the motion using computer vision. This allows the system to determine whether the performed movement matches the expected rehabilitation movement standard.

After motion analysis, the system checks whether the movement is correct. If the movement is correct, the system updates the patient’s score and proceeds to verify whether all required exercises have been completed. If not all exercises are completed, the patient continues performing the remaining exercises. If the movement is incorrect, the system displays a corrective prompt to guide the patient in adjusting their posture or movement before continuing the exercise. This creates a feedback loop that helps the patient improve exercise execution during the session.

Once all exercises are completed, the system marks the session as completed and generates performance data based on the patient’s activity. The system then records the adherence status, stores the performance data in the TheraQuest database, and displays the session results to the patient. The patient workflow ends after the results are presented.

For the **Physical Therapist workflow**, the system displays the therapist dashboard after successful login. From the dashboard, the therapist selects an action, such as assigning a rehabilitation program or viewing performance reports. When assigning a rehabilitation program, the system retrieves the necessary data from the TheraQuest database and displays the available rehabilitation programs. When viewing performance reports, the system retrieves stored performance and adherence data from the database and displays the generated reports. This allows the physical therapist to monitor patient progress, review exercise performance, and assess session-level adherence.

Overall, the flowchart shows that the TheraQuest VR system operates as an integrated rehabilitation support platform. It allows patients to perform guided VR-based exercises with real-time motion analysis and corrective feedback, while enabling physical therapists to manage rehabilitation programs and review patient performance through stored system-generated data.

### **3.6.2 System Architecture**

The system architecture presents the structural organization of the TheraQuest VR system and shows how its major layers and components work together to support virtual reality-based rehabilitation. It defines the flow of interaction from the user interface to system processing and data storage, ensuring that patient movements, therapist inputs, exercise evaluations, feedback responses, gamification elements, and adherence records are properly handled within the system. Through this architecture, the system is organized into clear layers that separate user interaction, application control, motion processing, and database management, making the TheraQuest VR system more structured, maintainable, and aligned with its rehabilitation objectives.

![][image8]

**Figure 3.6.2.1** Four-Layer System Architecture of the TheraQuest VR System

The system architecture diagram presents the TheraQuest VR system as a four layer structure that illustrates how system components interact to support rehabilitation processes. The layers are arranged vertically to show the flow of data and functionality, from user interaction at the top to data storage at the bottom.

The **Presentation Layer** represents the user interface of the system, where both the patient and the physical therapist interact with the platform. It includes the VR Environment, which delivers immersive rehabilitation exercises, the Gamification module, which displays scores, rewards, and progress indicators, and the Therapist Dashboard, which provides access to reports, monitoring tools, and system configuration.

The **Application Layer** serves as the control and coordination layer of the system. It manages user authentication to ensure secure access, session management to handle the start and tracking of rehabilitation activities, and program management to assign and configure exercises based on the therapist’s plan.

The **Processing Layer** functions as the core of the system, where movement data is analyzed and evaluated. The Motion Tracking module captures and interprets body movements in real time, which are then assessed by the Exercise Evaluation module to determine accuracy. Based on the results, the system generates real time feedback through the Feedback module and records session completion through the Adherence Monitoring module.

The **Data Layer** is responsible for storing and organizing all system data. It includes patient and session information, performance results, adherence records, and rehabilitation programs. This data supports progress tracking, report generation, and therapist decision making.

Overall, the architecture highlights how each layer works together to deliver a continuous flow of interaction, processing, feedback, and monitoring within the TheraQuest VR system.

### **3.6.3 System Components and Functional Modules**

The TheraQuest VR system consists of six core functional modules: VR Environment, Motion Tracking, Exercise Evaluation, Feedback Generation, Gamification, and Adherence Monitoring. These modules work together as interconnected components to support the rehabilitation process by capturing user input, analyzing movements, generating feedback, and recording performance data. Each module performs a specific function, contributing to accurate motion tracking, real time feedback, user engagement, and session level adherence monitoring, forming the core operation of the system.

#### **VR Environment Module**

![][image9]

**Figure 3.6.3.1** VR Environment Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The VR Environment Module serves as the primary interface through which the patient interacts with the TheraQuest system. It receives four categories of input: hardware signals from the VR headset such as the Meta Quest, physical gestures and head movements from the patient, exercise data loaded from the assigned rehabilitation program, and feedback signals passed in from the processing layer. These inputs are handled by four internal components operating in sequence within the Unity game engine.

The Scene Renderer is responsible for constructing and displaying the three-dimensional rehabilitation environment that the patient sees upon entering the VR session. The Interaction Controller captures all user actions performed within the virtual space, including hand movements, head orientation, and positional data, and forwards these to the motion tracking pipeline. The Exercise Prompt Display presents the current task instructions and movement cues to guide the patient through the prescribed rehabilitation activity. Finally, the Feedback Overlay renders the real-time visual and audio responses generated by the feedback module directly within the patient's VR view.

The outputs of this module include the fully rendered immersive scene, raw user movement data sent to the motion tracking module, exercise prompts displayed to the patient, and real-time corrective feedback delivered through the headset. Together, these outputs ensure that the patient receives a continuous, guided, and responsive rehabilitation experience throughout each session.

#### **Motion Tracking Module**

![][image10]

**Figure 3.6.3.2** Motion Tracking Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The Motion Tracking Module is responsible for capturing and interpreting the physical movements of the patient in real time. It receives input from three sources: camera sensors such as built-in VR cameras or external webcams, positional data from VR tracking hardware including controllers and headset orientation, and raw video frames streamed continuously during the session. These inputs are processed through a five-stage pipeline implemented using computer vision libraries such as OpenCV or MediaPipe in Python.

The Frame Preprocessor normalizes and denoises each incoming video frame to ensure consistent image quality before analysis. The Pose Estimator applies body landmark detection algorithms to identify the positions of key joints and body parts within each frame. The Joint Angle Calculator derives angular measurements from the detected keypoints, producing range-of-motion values for each relevant limb and joint involved in the exercise. The Movement Classifier compares the detected gesture patterns against known exercise types to determine which movement the patient is currently performing. The Motion Data Packager then formats all extracted information into a structured data object ready for downstream processing.

The outputs produced by this module include body keypoint coordinates representing landmark positions, joint angle data capturing range of motion values, and a fully processed motion data package transmitted to the exercise evaluation module. This pipeline ensures that all physical activity during the session is accurately captured and represented in a form suitable for objective performance assessment.

#### **Exercise Evaluation Module**

![][image11]

**Figure 3.6.3.3** Exercise Evaluation Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The Exercise Evaluation Module assesses the correctness and quality of the patient's movements by comparing real-time motion data against predefined rehabilitation standards. It receives three inputs: the processed motion data package from the motion tracking module, the rehabilitation movement standards configured by the physical therapist, and the exercise definition stored in the database which specifies the required movement criteria for each task. The module is implemented in C\# and operates in direct integration with the Unity game engine.

The Movement Validator compares the patient's current pose and motion trajectory against the expected movement standard for the active exercise. The Accuracy Scorer quantifies how closely the detected movement matches the required criteria and assigns a numerical correctness score. The Rep Counter tracks how many complete and valid repetitions of each exercise have been performed during the session. The Error Detector identifies specific deviations or incorrect movements and generates corresponding error flags that are forwarded to the feedback module. The Evaluation Result Packager consolidates all outputs into a structured result object for distribution to other modules and database storage.

The outputs of this module include an accuracy score for each exercise attempt, a repetition count reflecting session progress, error flags that trigger corrective guidance in the feedback module, and a complete evaluation result record that is stored in the Performance Record entity of the database. This module forms the objective core of the system's ability to assess patient rehabilitation performance consistently and without requiring direct therapist observation.

#### **Feedback Generation Module**

![][image12]

**Figure 3.6.3.4** Feedback Generation Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The Feedback Generation Module translates evaluation results into immediate, contextually relevant responses delivered to the patient within the VR environment. It receives evaluation results containing accuracy scores and error flags from the exercise evaluation module, specific joint deviation data identifying which body part performed incorrectly, and session context information indicating the current exercise and overall progress state.

The Feedback Decision Engine determines what type and priority of feedback is appropriate based on the incoming evaluation data, distinguishing between confirmatory feedback for correct movements and corrective feedback for errors. The Visual Cue Generator produces in-VR overlays and highlights that guide the patient's attention toward the area requiring correction or affirm correct execution. The Audio Prompt Generator produces voice instructions and sound responses delivered through the headset's audio output, reinforcing the visual cues with spoken guidance. The Corrective Instruction Engine generates specific movement adjustment instructions tailored to the identified error, helping the patient understand what change in posture or motion is required.

The outputs of this module include visual overlays rendered within the VR scene, audio prompts delivered through the headset, and corrective guidance text that is also logged to the performance database for clinical reference. By delivering all three feedback types simultaneously and in real time, this module ensures that patients receive continuous and actionable guidance throughout each rehabilitation exercise without requiring the physical presence of the therapist.

#### **Gamification Module**

![][image13]

**Figure 3.6.3.5** Gamification Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The Gamification Module integrates interactive game-based mechanics into the rehabilitation experience to sustain patient motivation and encourage consistent participation. It receives accuracy scores from the exercise evaluation module, repetition counts reflecting the number of completed exercise cycles, and session progress data indicating the current state of exercise completion within the assigned program. The module is implemented in C\# within the Unity game engine.

The Score Calculator converts accuracy scores and repetition counts into a quantified point value that reflects the patient's performance quality for the current session. The Reward Engine determines which incentives, such as badges, stars, or achievement markers, have been earned based on the session score and distributes them accordingly within the VR interface. The Progression Controller manages the advancement of rehabilitation difficulty and exercise sequencing, adjusting the level or complexity of subsequent tasks in response to the patient's demonstrated performance. The HUD Display Manager renders all gamification elements, including the live score counter, reward notifications, and progression indicators, directly within the patient's VR heads-up display.

The outputs of this module include the session score displayed in the VR interface, unlocked rewards shown to the patient upon task completion, a next-level trigger that advances the exercise difficulty when performance thresholds are met, and a progress summary stored to the session record in the database. By embedding these motivational mechanics within the rehabilitation workflow, the module transforms routine therapy exercises into a goal-oriented and engaging activity that supports long-term patient adherence.

#### **Adherence Monitoring Module**

![][image14]

**Figure 3.6.3.6** Adherence Monitoring Module of the TheraQuest VR System

The Adherence Monitoring Module evaluates whether the patient has completed the prescribed rehabilitation session as assigned by the physical therapist and generates compliance records for clinical review. It receives three inputs: session data including start time and end time, exercise completion data reflecting repetition counts and done status for each task, and the prescribed program definition specifying the full list of required exercises for the session.

The Completion Checker verifies whether all exercises included in the assigned rehabilitation program have been performed during the session. The Status Classifier categorizes the session outcome as complete, incomplete, or missed based on the verification results, providing a clear and standardized label for each session record. The Adherence Record Writer saves the classified result to the Adherence Record entity in the database, linking the outcome to both the patient identifier and the corresponding session identifier. The Report Generator compiles all adherence data from the session into a structured summary formatted for presentation on the physical therapist's monitoring dashboard.

The outputs of this module include a completion flag indicating whether the session passed or failed the prescribed requirements, a session status label classifying the outcome, a saved adherence record stored in the database, and a therapist report delivered to the dashboard for clinical monitoring. This module focuses strictly on session-level compliance and does not analyze long-term behavioral patterns, ensuring that the system provides the therapist with an accurate and objective record of whether each assigned rehabilitation session was carried out as required.

## **3.7 System Development and Implementation**

System development and implementation describe the process of transforming the system design into a functional TheraQuest VR prototype. This section presents the hardware and software requirements, class diagram, and testing procedures used to support the development of the system. It explains how the planned components, including the VR environment, motion tracking, exercise evaluation, feedback generation, gamification, adherence monitoring, and database management, are implemented and tested to ensure that the system operates according to its intended rehabilitation objectives.

### **3.7.1 Hardware and Software Requirements**

This section outlines the hardware and software components required for the development and operation of the TheraQuest VR system. These requirements ensure that the system can effectively support virtual reality interaction, real-time motion tracking, and data processing for rehabilitation monitoring.

#### **Hardware Requirements**

The system requires a **VR headset**, such as the Meta Quest, to provide an immersive virtual environment where patients can perform rehabilitation exercises. The headset enables users to interact with the system in a three-dimensional space, enhancing engagement and simulating guided therapy sessions.

A **computer system** is necessary to run the application, process data, and handle the integration of VR and computer vision components. The computer should have sufficient processing power, including a capable CPU and GPU, to support real-time rendering and motion analysis without delays or performance issues.

The system also requires **camera sensors** to capture user movements for motion tracking. These sensors, which may include **built-in VR tracking cameras or external webcams**, are used in conjunction with computer vision algorithms to detect body posture and movement. Accurate sensor input is essential for evaluating exercise performance.

An **adequate physical space** is required to ensure safe and effective use of the system. Users must have enough room to move freely while performing exercises without obstruction. This space also contributes to **accurate motion tracking** by minimizing environmental interference.

#### **Software Requirements**

The development of the system utilizes the **Unity engine**, which serves as the primary platform for building the VR environment. Unity supports the creation of interactive 3D applications and enables integration with VR hardware, making it suitable for developing immersive rehabilitation scenarios.

For motion tracking and analysis, the system uses computer vision libraries such as **OpenCV** or **MediaPipe,** or any similar libraries. These tools provide functionalities for detecting and interpreting human body movements, including pose estimation and gesture recognition, which are essential for evaluating exercise accuracy.

Programming languages such as **C\#** and **Python** is used in system development. **C\#** is primarily used within Unity for implementing system logic, user interaction, and gamification features, while Python is used for computer vision processing and integration of motion tracking algorithms.

A **database system** is required to store and manage system data, including patient information, session records, performance metrics, and adherence results. The database ensures that data is securely stored and can be retrieved efficiently by the system, particularly for monitoring and reporting purposes by physical therapist.

### **3.7.2 Class Diagram**

The class diagram illustrates the structural design of the TheraQuest VR system by defining the system’s classes, their attributes, methods, and relationships. It provides a detailed representation of how data and functionalities are organized within the system, reflecting the underlying object-oriented design used during development. Each class corresponds to a key component of the system, such as user management, rehabilitation sessions, motion tracking, performance evaluation, and adherence monitoring. The relationships between classes, including associations and dependencies, demonstrate how different components interact to support system operations. This diagram serves as a blueprint for system implementation, ensuring that all functional requirements are properly translated into a well-structured and maintainable software architecture.

*![][image15]*

**Figure 3.7.2.1** Class Diagram of the TheraQuest VR System

The **PhysicalTherapist** class represents the licensed physical therapist who manages the rehabilitation process. Based on the diagram, one physical therapist can be associated with multiple patients, while each patient is assigned to one physical therapist. This reflects the role of the therapist in supervising and monitoring patients throughout their rehabilitation activities.

The **PhysicalTherapist** class is also connected to the **RehabilitationProgram** class. This means that one physical therapist can create or manage multiple rehabilitation programs, while each rehabilitation program is created or assigned by one physical therapist. This supports the system’s function of allowing therapists to prepare structured exercise programs for patients.

The **Patient** class represents the user who performs rehabilitation exercises using the VR system. A patient is connected to the **Session** class, indicating that one patient can have multiple rehabilitation sessions, while each session belongs to one patient. This allows the system to record and monitor the patient’s rehabilitation activities over time.

The **Patient** class is also associated with the **RehabilitationProgram** class. This relationship indicates that a patient is assigned a rehabilitation program that serves as the basis for the exercises performed during the VR rehabilitation session. This ensures that the patient follows a structured therapy plan provided by the physical therapist.

The **RehabilitationProgram** class represents the complete set of prescribed rehabilitation activities. It is connected to the **Exercise** class, showing that one rehabilitation program may contain multiple exercises, while each exercise belongs to one rehabilitation program. This structure allows the system to organize different exercises under a specific therapy program.

The **Exercise** class represents an individual rehabilitation activity within a program. It contains the movement instructions and required standards used during exercise performance. The exercise data are used by the system as the basis for evaluating whether the patient’s movements are correct or incorrect during a session.

The **Session** class represents an actual VR rehabilitation session performed by the patient. It is connected to the **Exercise** class, indicating that a session includes one or more exercises that the patient must complete. The session serves as the central activity record where exercise performance, completion status, and generated results are linked.

The **PerformanceRecord** class stores the results generated from the patient’s exercise performance. Based on the diagram, one session can generate multiple performance records, while each performance record belongs to one session. These records may include accuracy scores, detected errors, repetition counts, feedback results, and timestamps. This class supports the system’s ability to produce performance summaries for therapist review.

The **AdherenceRecord** class stores the completion status of the rehabilitation session. It is connected to the **Session** class, showing that each session has an adherence record that identifies whether the prescribed rehabilitation activities were completed or not. This supports the adherence monitoring function of the system by providing objective session-level compliance data.

The **VRSystem** class represents the main system controller of TheraQuest VR. It coordinates the overall operation of the system, including user access, rehabilitation session execution, motion tracking, exercise evaluation, feedback generation, gamification, performance recording, and adherence monitoring. It acts as the central controller that connects the different classes into one functional rehabilitation platform.

Overall, the class diagram shows that the TheraQuest VR system is structured around the interaction between the physical therapist and the patient. The physical therapist creates rehabilitation programs, the patient performs exercises through VR sessions, and the system records performance and adherence data. This structure supports the system’s objectives of guided VR-based rehabilitation, motion evaluation, real-time feedback, and therapist monitoring.

### **3.7.3 System Testing**

The TheraQuest VR system undergoes system testing to ensure that all parts of the system function correctly and work together as intended. This phase verifies that the virtual environment, motion tracking, feedback, and monitoring features operate properly and support the goals of the rehabilitation process. System testing is necessary to identify issues, confirm correct system behavior, and ensure that users can interact with the system without difficulty.

**Functional testing** is performed to check whether each feature of the system meets the required specifications. This includes testing actions such as starting a session, performing exercises, receiving feedback, and viewing progress. Each component is tested individually and as part of the complete system to ensure proper operation and correct flow of data.

**Motion tracking accuracy testing** is conducted to determine how well the system detects and interprets user movements. The system compares the user’s movements with the expected exercise patterns to check if the movements are correctly identified. This ensures that the system can accurately recognize correct and incorrect actions during rehabilitation.

**System responsiveness testing** evaluates how quickly the system responds to user actions. Since the system provides immediate feedback during exercises, responses such as visual and audio cues must be delivered without delay. This helps maintain smooth interaction and supports effective guidance during therapy sessions.

The testing process also includes debugging and error correction. During this stage, any problems such as incorrect results, system interruptions, or unexpected behavior are identified and resolved. Adjustments are made to improve system performance and ensure stable operation.

## **3.8 System Evaluation**

This section presents the procedures used to evaluate the **TheraQuest VR** system after development and implementation. The evaluation focuses on determining the system’s usability, motion tracking accuracy, adherence monitoring functionality, and relevance as a rehabilitation support tool. It involves healthy volunteers for system testing and refinement, physical therapy patients for final usability testing, and licensed physical therapists for expert evaluation of the system-generated adherence reports and performance summaries.

Data are gathered through system-generated records, observation checklists, usability questionnaires, and expert evaluation forms. These data include motion tracking results, exercise performance, session completion status, adherence records, and feedback outputs. Overall, this section ensures that the system is evaluated in a structured, safe, and ethical manner based on both technical performance and user-centered assessment.

### **3.8.1 Research Locale**

The study is conducted in a controlled environment specifically arranged to support virtual reality (VR)-based interaction, ensuring adequate space, participant safety, and minimal external interference. Such conditions are necessary to facilitate accurate motion tracking and effective user engagement within the VR rehabilitation system.

The research is implemented within a selected medical institution in Butuan City, Agusan del Norte, Philippines, with the assistance and supervision of licensed physical therapists. This setting provides a clinically appropriate environment that reflects standard rehabilitation practices, thereby enhancing the validity and applicability of the study.

All technical equipment required for the implementation of the TheraQuest VR system, including VR headsets, computer systems, and motion tracking devices, is supplied and maintained by the researchers. The medical institution functions solely as the research venue and does not provide the equipment used in the study. This arrangement ensures consistency in system configuration and performance throughout the data collection process.

Furthermore, appropriate spatial layout and lighting conditions are maintained to optimize computer vision accuracy and overall system usability. The involvement of physical therapy professionals ensures that all procedures are conducted safely and in accordance with established rehabilitation protocols.

Overall, the selected research locale provides a controlled and clinically relevant environment that supports reliable data collection and comprehensive evaluation of the system’s effectiveness in facilitating rehabilitation and adherence monitoring. 

### **3.8.2 Research Participants**

The participants of the study consist of three groups: physical therapy patients, healthy volunteers, and licensed physical therapists (PT doctors). These participants are selected using purposive sampling based on their relevance to the study and their ability to interact with or evaluate the system.

A total of **5 to 10 physical therapy patients** will participate in the study. Their involvement is limited to the final system testing and evaluation phase to ensure that participation does not interfere with their ongoing or future rehabilitation. During this phase, patients will use the system to perform prescribed exercises, allowing the researchers to assess usability, safety, and system effectiveness in a real rehabilitation setting.

In addition, **5 to 10 healthy volunteers** will be involved during the development and testing phases of the system. These participants will assist in the iterative refinement of the system by performing simulated rehabilitation exercises and providing feedback on usability, interaction, and responsiveness. They are selected based on their ability to perform motor movements aligned with the required rehabilitation exercises, enabling accurate testing of motion tracking, feedback mechanisms, and overall system functionality without risking patient safety.

Furthermore, **3 to 5 licensed physical therapists (PT doctors)** will participate as expert evaluators. They will assess the usefulness, effectiveness, and clinical relevance of the system, particularly the adherence monitoring component. PT doctors will review system-generated outputs such as adherence reports and performance summaries to determine whether the system provides accurate and meaningful data that can support rehabilitation monitoring and clinical decision-making.

The inclusion of these participant groups ensures a comprehensive evaluation of the system. Healthy volunteers contribute to system development and technical validation, physical therapy patients provide real-world usability testing, and PT doctors offer expert assessment of the system’s clinical applicability and effectiveness.

### **3.8.3 Research Instrument**

This study uses research instruments that directly correspond to the major evaluation areas of the TheraQuest VR system. These instruments are used to gather data on motion tracking accuracy, adherence monitoring, system usability, and expert evaluation of the system-generated outputs.

#### **Motion Tracking Accuracy**

Motion tracking accuracy is evaluated using system-generated motion tracking records collected during the performance of VR-based rehabilitation exercises. These records include movement classification results, expected and detected joint coordinates, and expected and detected joint angles.

The collected data are used to determine how accurately the system detects and interprets user movements. Specifically, the motion tracking records serve as the basis for computing the confusion matrix, Euclidean distance error, and angle error. These measurements help determine whether the system can correctly identify correct and incorrect movements and whether the detected body positions are aligned with the expected rehabilitation movement standards.

#### **Adherence Monitoring System**

The adherence monitoring system is evaluated based on its ability to record and present session-level completion data. The system-generated adherence records include the session status, completion result, exercise completion data, and performance summary generated after the rehabilitation session.

This instrument focuses on determining whether the system can properly identify if a prescribed rehabilitation session was completed, incomplete, or missed. The recorded adherence data are used to assess the functionality and usefulness of the system in supporting rehabilitation monitoring.

#### **Evaluation Statements for Physical Therapists**

The evaluation statements for physical therapists are used to gather expert feedback regarding the adherence monitoring component of the TheraQuest VR system. Licensed physical therapists answer the statements using a five-point Likert scale ranging from Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree.

The evaluation focuses on the accuracy of session completion recording, clarity of adherence reports, relevance of the provided information, usefulness in monitoring patient progress, and overall acceptability of the adherence monitoring component. The responses are used to determine whether the adherence monitoring system provides meaningful and practical support for physical therapy monitoring.

#### **System Usability**

System usability is evaluated using the System Usability Scale (SUS). This instrument consists of ten standardized questions answered through a five-point Likert scale. It measures the participants’ perception of the system’s ease of use, learnability, consistency, and overall usability.

The SUS helps determine whether users can interact with the TheraQuest VR system comfortably and effectively. The results are used to assess whether the system interface, VR interaction, and overall workflow are acceptable for its intended users.

#### **Expert Evaluation of System Outputs**

Expert evaluation of system outputs is conducted by licensed physical therapists to assess the quality and clinical relevance of the system-generated reports. This includes the review of adherence reports, performance summaries, accuracy results, and other outputs produced by the system after a rehabilitation session.

The evaluation determines whether the generated outputs are clear, useful, relevant, and acceptable for supporting rehabilitation monitoring and clinical decision-making. The responses from physical therapists provide expert validation of whether the system outputs can assist in reviewing patient performance and adherence within the scope of the study.

#### **Data Gathering Procedures**

The data gathering process is conducted in a structured sequence to ensure consistency and reliability of collected data.

First, participants are given an **orientation session**, where they are introduced to the purpose of the study, the functionality of the TheraQuest VR system, and the proper use of the VR equipment. Instructions on how to perform the rehabilitation exercises are also provided.

Following the orientation, participants proceed to **perform VR-based rehabilitation exercises** using the system. During this phase, they interact with the virtual environment while executing prescribed movements.

While the participants are performing the tasks, the system automatically **records performance data**, including motion tracking accuracy, movement evaluation results, and adherence monitoring outputs. At the same time, researchers utilize an observation checklist to monitor user interaction and note any usability issues or behavioral responses.

After completing the session, participants are asked to **answer the survey questionnaires**, including the System Usability Scale (SUS) and the user feedback questionnaire, to evaluate their experience with the system.

Finally, all collected data, including system-generated logs, observation records, and questionnaire responses are compiled for analysis to assess the system’s accuracy, usability, and the functionality and relevance of its adherence monitoring component.

## **3.9 Data Analysis**

Data gathered in this study will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and system performance evaluation metrics to assess motion-tracking accuracy, adherence-monitoring functionality, usability, and clinical relevance of the TheraQuest VR system. The data sources include system-generated performance logs, observation checklist results, System Usability Scale (SUS) responses, user feedback questionnaires, and expert evaluations from licensed physical therapists. Quantitative data will be organized, tabulated, and computed using Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets, while motion tracking metrics may also be processed using Python when necessary. These methods are suitable because the study involves both questionnaire-based responses and objective system-generated measures, including accuracy scores, repetition counts, detected errors, and session completion records.

### **3.9.1 Motion Tracking Accuracy**

 The study will use a **Confusion matrix, Euclidean distance error,** and **Angle error**. The confusion matrix will be used to determine how accurately the system classifies user movements as correct or incorrect.

1. #### **Confusion Matrix**

From the confusion matrix, the following metrics will be computed: 

**Accuracy** will be computed using the formula:

**$Accuracy=\ \frac{TP\ +\ TN}{TP\ +\ TN\ +\ FP\ +\ FN}$**

**Precision** will be computed using**:**

**$Precision\ =\ \frac{TP\ }{TP\ +\ FP}$**

**Recall** will be computed using**:**

**${}$$Recall=\ \frac{TP\ }{TP\ +\ FN}$**

And the **F1-score** will be computed using**:**

**$F1\ Score=\ \frac{2(Precision\ \times \ Recall)}{Precision\ +\ Recall\ }$**

Where:

* **TP \= True Positives**  
* **TN \= True Negatives**  
* **FP \= False Positives**  
* **FN \= False Negatives**

To provide a basis for interpretation, the study will adopt the following minimum acceptance benchmark for motion classification performance:

| Metric | Minimum Acceptable Value | Interpretation |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Accuracy** | **85% or higher** | Acceptable overall classification performance |
| **Precision** | **80% or higher** | Acceptable correctness of positive detections |
| **Recall** | **80% or higher** | Acceptable ability to detect the required correct movements |
| **F1-Score** | **80% or higher** | Acceptable balance between precision and recall |

**Table 2**. Minimum Acceptance Value Metric Table for Confusion Matrix

The percentage score for each classification metric is derived from the confusion matrix by substituting the values of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives into the appropriate formula and multiplying the result by 100\. The resulting percentage is then compared with the predefined minimum acceptable value to determine whether system performance is satisfactory. The benchmark values were set by the researchers as minimum acceptable system performance criteria for prototype evaluation.

2. #### **Euclidean Distance Error**

To measure the positional difference between the detected and expected joint coordinates, the **Euclidean distance error** will be used. Since the system operates within a three-dimensional VR environment and utilizes positional tracking data from VR hardware together with computer vision-based body landmark detection, motion tracking accuracy may be evaluated using the t**hree-dimensional Euclidean distance formula**.

For **three-dimensional coordinates**, the formula is:

$d\ =\ \sqrt{{\left({{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}\right)}^{2}+{\left({{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}\right)}^{2}+{\left({{z}_{2}-{z}_{1}}\right)}^{2}}$

Where:

* **$\left({{x}_{1},\ {y}_{1},\ {z}_{1}}\right)$** **\= expected joint position**  
* $\left({{x}_{2},\ {y}_{2},\ {z}_{2}}\right)$ **\= detected joint position**   
* $d$   **\=  distance error**

The **expected coordinate anchor** will be based on the **predefined reference coordinates** of the correct rehabilitation posture or movement standard established in the system. These reference coordinates serve as the baseline against which detected body joint positions are compared.

| Measure | Acceptable Threshold |
| :---: | :---: |
| Euclidean Distance Error | **Within the therapist-defined tolerance level** |

**Table 3**. Acceptable Threshold of Measurement of the Euclidean Distance Error

The expected output for each tracked joint is the predefined reference coordinate corresponding to the correct exercise posture. The detected coordinate is considered acceptable when its Euclidean distance from the reference coordinate falls within the allowable tolerance level established for the system based on the standard set by the Physical Therapists. Lower Euclidean distance values indicate closer alignment with the expected rehabilitation standard.

3. #### **Angle Error**

Angle error will be used to measure the difference between the **expected joint angle** and the **detected joint angle** during exercise performance. This is important in rehabilitation exercises where correct posture and range of motion depend on proper joint alignment. 

**Angle error** will be computed using the formula:

$Angle\ Error\ =\ \left|{{\Theta }_{expected}-{\Theta }_{detected}\ }\right|$

Where:

* ​ ${\Theta }_{expected}{\ }$ \= represents the **expected joint angle** based on the prescribed rehabilitation movement.  
*  ${\Theta }_{detected}$ \= represents the **actual joint angle** detected by the system.

A lower angle error indicates closer agreement between the performed movement and the expected posture. For interpretation, the detected movement may be considered acceptable if the angle error is within **${5}^{°}$** to **${10}^{°}$** degrees of the expected joint angle, depending on the allowable tolerance established for the exercise.

### **3.9.2 Adherence Monitoring System**

The adherence monitoring component of the system will be evaluated in terms of its functionality, usefulness, and relevance in supporting rehabilitation monitoring. Licensed physical therapists will assess the system-generated adherence reports using a structured evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. The evaluation will focus on the accuracy of session completion recording, clarity of reports, and usefulness in clinical monitoring and decision-making.

**Weighted Mean:**

$\overline{X\ }=\ \frac{\Sigma fx}{N}$

**Percentage:**

$Percentage\ =\ \frac{f}{N}\ \times \ 100$

**Percentage Agreement:**

$Percentage\ Agreement\ =\ \frac{Number\ of\ Agreements}{Total\ Number\ of\ Cases}\times \ 100$

Where:

* $\overline{X}$ \= weighted mean  
* $f$ \= frequency  
* $x$ \= Likert scale value  
* $N$ \= total number of responses

#### **Likert Scale for Adherence Monitoring Evaluation**

| Scale | Verbal Interpretation |
| :---: | :---: |
| 5 | Strongly Agree |
| 4 | Agree |
| 3 | Neutral |
| 2 | Disagree |
| 1 | Strongly Disagree |

### **3.9.3 System Usability**

Usability of the system is evaluated using the **System Usability Scale (SUS)**, with scores interpreted according to standard SUS guidelines. Observation checklist data are also analyzed to identify usability issues encountered during system interaction.

For odd-numbered items:

$Score\ =\ Response\ -\ 1$

For even-numbered items:

$Score\ =\ 5\ -\ Response$

For the Final Scoring:

$SUS\ SCORE\ =\ \left({\sum\limits_{}^{}Adjusted\ Scores}\right)\ \times \ 2.5$

## **3.10 Ethical Considerations**

to protect the rights, safety, and well-being of all participants. Before participation, all individuals are provided with a clear explanation of the study’s purpose, procedures, and expected involvement. Participants are required to give informed consent, indicating their voluntary agreement to take part in the study.

Participation in the study is entirely voluntary, and participants have the right to withdraw at any time without penalty. For physical therapy patients, extra care is taken to ensure that their involvement does not interfere with their ongoing treatment or cause any physical discomfort. All activities are conducted under the supervision of licensed physical therapists to ensure safety during VR-based rehabilitation exercises.

Confidentiality and data privacy are strictly maintained throughout the study. Personal information and collected data, including performance records and adherence reports, are securely stored and used solely for research purposes. Participant identities are anonymized in all reports and publications to protect their privacy.

Additionally, the study ensures that the use of VR equipment and motion tracking systems does not pose any harm to participants. Proper orientation and safety guidelines are provided before system use, and the research environment is controlled to minimize risks. Overall, the study upholds ethical responsibility by prioritizing participant welfare, informed participation, and secure data handling.
